title: THE FIRST MAN IN THE BIBLE TO TAKE TWO WIVES ALSO BRAGGED ABOUT KILLING A MAN—AND HIS WORDS EXPOSE SOMETHING TERRIFYING ABOUT THE HUMAN HEART
paragraphs: THE FIRST MAN IN THE BIBLE TO TAKE TWO WIVES ALSO BRAGGED ABOUT KILLING A MAN—AND HIS WORDS EXPOSE SOMETHING TERRIFYING ABOUT THE HUMAN HEART

Before the flood, before the Ten Commandments, and long before humanity learned to celebrate its own rebellion, one man gathered his two wives and delivered a chilling speech. What he said reveals how sin can turn a wounded heart into a dangerous one—and why the world still desperately needs Jesus Christ.
There is something deeply disturbing about a man who can speak of taking another human life without a trace of remorse.
But perhaps even more disturbing is a man who turns that violence into poetry.
He doesn't whisper his confession.
He doesn't fall to his knees.
He doesn't ask God for mercy.
He calls his wives together.
And he tells them to listen.
His name was Lamech.
And buried in the fourth chapter of Genesis is one of the earliest recorded human speeches after the fall—a speech so dark that thousands of years later, it still sounds frighteningly familiar.
Because Lamech wasn't merely talking about violence.
He was revealing what happens when a human being begins to treat his own pride as more important than another person's life.
And before you decide this ancient man has nothing to do with you, consider something.
Have you ever been hurt so deeply that you secretly wanted someone else to hurt just as badly?
Have you ever rehearsed an argument in your head, imagining the perfect words that would finally make someone regret what they did to you?
Have you ever called something justice when, somewhere deep inside, you knew it was revenge?
Stay with me.
Because this story begins with two wives and a disturbing declaration.
But it leads us to a question that reaches into our marriages, our families, our churches, our hidden resentments, and the places in our hearts we rarely allow anyone to see.
What happens when a wounded person decides that revenge is more important than mercy?
And what happens when that person is us?
Genesis 4:19 tells us:
"And Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah." — Genesis 4:19, KJV
At first glance, it might seem like a simple family record.
One man.
Two women.
A household.
But Genesis is not giving us this information without context.
The Bible has already introduced God's design for marriage.
In Genesis 2:24, a man leaves his father and mother, cleaves to his wife, and the two become one flesh.
One man.
One woman.
One covenant union.
Then, only two chapters later, Scripture introduces Lamech, the first man explicitly recorded as taking two wives.
The Hebrew says:
וַיִּקַּח־לוֹ לֶמֶךְ שְׁתֵּי נָשִׁים
Vayyiqqaḥ-lo Lemekh shtei nashim.
Literally, in context:
"And Lamech took for himself two wives."
Notice the expression shtei nashim.
Two wives.

The text does not tell us what Adah and Zillah felt about this arrangement. It does not describe their marriage as a romantic success, nor does it explicitly record God condemning Lamech in that verse.
But placed against the marriage pattern established in Genesis 2, this is a significant development.
Humanity is already moving away from the beginning God declared good.
And the narrator is about to show us something even darker.
Because Lamech's household was not without accomplishments.
His descendants are associated with livestock keeping, musical instruments, and metalworking.
Genesis 4:20–22 introduces Jabal, Jubal, and Tubal-cain.
There is cultural development here.
Skill.
Creativity.
Industry.
The ability to cultivate the world and produce things of beauty and usefulness.
And that detail matters.
Because the Bible is showing us something we still struggle to understand.
A civilization can become more sophisticated without becoming more righteous.
A person can become extraordinarily talented without becoming humble.
A family can become financially successful without becoming spiritually healthy.
A society can develop remarkable technology while remaining morally broken.
And a man can build an impressive life while his heart is being consumed by pride.
We see versions of this everywhere.
People who can manage companies but cannot manage their anger.
People who know how to influence thousands but do not know how to apologize to one person.
People who can explain Scripture beautifully yet refuse to forgive someone who offended them.
People whose public lives look impressive while their private relationships are falling apart.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility is that we can become so occupied with what we are building that we stop noticing what we are becoming.
Then Lamech opens his mouth.
And the story changes.
"And Lamech said unto his wives, Adah and Zillah, Hear my voice; ye wives of Lamech, hearken unto my speech: for I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt." — Genesis 4:23, KJV
Read that again.
He is addressing the two women closest to him.
Adah.
Zillah.
Listen to me.
Hear what I have to say.
And then comes the declaration.
"I have slain a man."
The Hebrew reads:
כִּי אִישׁ הָרַגְתִּי לְפִצְעִי וְיֶלֶד לְחַבֻּרָתִי
Ki ish haragti lefits'i, veyeled leḥabburati.
The Hebrew expresses Lamech's claim that he has killed a man in connection with his wound and a young man in connection with his injury or bruise.
The exact circumstances are not given.

Some interpreters understand the two descriptions as referring poetically to one victim. Others see the possibility of two victims. The Hebrew parallelism makes the one-victim reading plausible, but the text does not settle every detail.

We also cannot establish whether the killing happened in self-defense, retaliation, or another circumstance. The wording associates the killing with an injury Lamech received, but it does not give us a complete account of the event.
What we can see is the posture of his speech.
There is no recorded confession of wrongdoing.
No appeal for God's forgiveness.
No expression of sorrow over a life lost.
Instead, his words move toward an extraordinary declaration about vengeance.
"If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold." — Genesis 4:24, KJV
There it is.
The chilling climax.
But to understand why this is so disturbing, we must remember who Cain was.
Cain had murdered his brother Abel.
The first recorded human murder arose within a family.
Not between strangers.
Not on a battlefield.
Between brothers.
And when God confronted Cain, Cain was judged.
Yet even after Cain's terrible sin, God placed a mark upon him and warned that anyone who killed him would face sevenfold vengeance.
That protection was God's declaration.
It was not Cain giving himself permission to murder again.
It was not an invitation for human beings to establish their own systems of unlimited retaliation.
It was God's prerogative to judge and restrain further bloodshed.
Now listen to Lamech.
Cain was promised sevenfold vengeance.
Lamech announces seventy-sevenfold.
The Hebrew says:
כִּי שִׁבְעָתַיִם יֻקַּם־קָיִן וְלֶמֶךְ שִׁבְעִים וְשִׁבְעָה
Ki shiv'atayim yuqqam-Qayin, veLemekh shiv'im veshiv'ah.
In context:
"If Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy-sevenfold."
The numbers function within a poetic declaration of intensified vengeance. They should not be treated as a mathematical formula establishing exactly how much punishment anyone deserved.
And we should not pretend that Lamech had received the same divine promise given to Cain.
Genesis records no such promise to Lamech.
What we hear is a man invoking Cain's protection and escalating the language of vengeance around himself.
A man speaking as though his injuries justify an extraordinary response.
A man whose words make his own wounded pride sound terrifyingly powerful.
And this is where the ancient story begins to walk into our homes.
Because most of us will never stand before our families and boast that we have killed someone.
But revenge does not always begin with bloodshed.
Sometimes it begins with a sentence.
"I'll make sure they regret what they did."
Sometimes it begins with silence.
"I'll never speak to them again, and I want them to suffer because of it."
Sometimes it begins with a social media post designed to humiliate someone without naming them.
Sometimes it begins with a parent who uses cruel words against a child because the parent feels disrespected.
Sometimes it begins with a husband or wife who keeps bringing up an old failure, not to resolve the wound, but to maintain power over the other person.
Sometimes it begins inside a church.
A disagreement becomes an offense.
An offense becomes resentment.
Resentment becomes a campaign to destroy someone's reputation.
And somehow, the person seeking revenge convinces themselves that God must be on their side.
That is the danger.
Not every desire for justice is sinful. Scripture repeatedly calls God's people to protect the vulnerable, confront evil, and pursue what is right.
Abuse must not be excused. Crimes should be addressed through appropriate authorities. Forgiveness does not require someone to remain in danger or abandon wise boundaries.
But there is a difference between seeking justice and worshiping revenge.
Justice asks what is right.
Revenge can become obsessed with making another person suffer.
Justice recognizes moral boundaries.
Revenge is tempted to cross them.
Justice can entrust final judgment to God.
Revenge wants to sit on the throne itself.
And sometimes the hardest spiritual truth to accept is this:
The fact that someone genuinely hurt you does not mean every response you desire is righteous.
Perhaps someone betrayed your trust.
Perhaps someone spread lies about you.
Perhaps someone abandoned you when you needed them most.
Perhaps you are still carrying words spoken years ago by a person who has never apologized.
Your pain may be real.
Your grief may be justified.
The injustice may have been serious.
God does not require you to pretend otherwise.
But pain can become dangerous when it begins demanding permission to become cruel.
That is why Lamech's speech matters.
It exposes how easily the human heart can turn a wound into a weapon.
And then Scripture gives us a contrast so beautiful that it is almost impossible to miss once you see it.
Centuries later, Peter approached Jesus with a question about forgiveness.
"Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?" — Matthew 18:21, KJV
Peter probably thought he was being generous.
Seven times.
Surely that was enough.
But Jesus answered:
"I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven." — Matthew 18:22, KJV
Now look carefully.
Lamech speaks of vengeance seventy-sevenfold.
Jesus speaks of forgiveness using language of overwhelming abundance.
In Greek, Matthew 18:22 includes the expression:
ἕως ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά
Heōs hebdomēkontakis hepta.

This expression is traditionally translated "seventy times seven," as in the King James Version. It is also understood by many scholars as "seventy-seven times," reflecting the Greek rendering of Genesis 4:24 in the Septuagint.
The precise numerical rendering is debated, but Jesus' meaning in context is clear.
He is not giving Peter a forgiveness counter.
He is confronting the desire to calculate the point at which mercy may finally be exhausted.
And the literary connection to Lamech's words is striking.
Where Lamech's speech magnifies vengeance, Jesus teaches His disciples to practice forgiveness beyond petty calculation.
Where the ancient boast centers on the wounded self, Jesus calls His followers toward a mercy shaped by the kingdom of heaven.
Think about that.
One man says, in effect, "My injury deserves multiplied vengeance."
Jesus teaches His disciples to forgive again and again.
One voice represents the escalation of human retaliation.
The other calls sinners into the radically different life of God's kingdom.
But Jesus did not merely deliver beautiful teaching about forgiveness.
He walked toward a cross.
And there, the contrast becomes almost unbearable.
Imagine the scene.
The Son of God has been betrayed.
Falsely accused.
Mocked.
Struck.
Scourged.
Crowned with thorns.
Nailed to wood.
He is not suffering because He committed some hidden crime.
He is the righteous One suffering at the hands of sinners.
And while the people around Him are committing an unspeakable injustice, Luke records these words:
"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." — Luke 23:34, KJV

Some early manuscripts omit this sentence, a textual question noted in modern Bible editions. Nevertheless, the prayer is deeply consistent with Jesus' teaching on loving enemies and with the wider New Testament witness to His mercy.
Consider the contrast.
Lamech calls his wives to hear about his vengeance.
Jesus, suffering on the cross, prays for His persecutors.
Lamech's words center on the injury done to him.
Jesus' words reveal mercy even in the face of terrible injustice.
Lamech speaks of multiplied vengeance.
Jesus bears the judgment our sins deserve so that guilty people may receive forgiveness through Him.
And this is where we must be careful not to reduce Christianity to a simple lesson about being nicer to people.
The Gospel is far greater than anger management.
Jesus did not come merely to teach violent people to become peaceful or bitter people to become pleasant.
He came to save sinners.
People like Cain.
People like Lamech.
People like Peter, who would later deny Him.
People like the thief dying beside Him.
People like you.
People like me.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had fixed everything.
Not after we had made ourselves worthy.
Not after we had learned how to hide our worst failures behind a respectable appearance.
While we were still sinners.
That is grace.
But grace is not permission to continue embracing evil.
It is God's undeserved favor calling us away from sin and into new life through Jesus Christ.
And perhaps someone reading this is realizing that the deepest problem in their life is not merely what another person did to them.
It is what their own heart has become while carrying that wound.
Maybe bitterness has become your daily companion.
Maybe you have grown comfortable wishing disaster on someone.
Maybe you have been justifying words you know were cruel.
Maybe you have been hiding behind the sentence, "But you don't understand what they did to me."
And perhaps nobody does understand the full weight of what happened.
But Jesus does not need to misunderstand your suffering in order to challenge your response to it.
He knows what betrayal feels like.
He knows what false accusation looks like.
He knows what it means to be abandoned by people who promised to remain faithful.
And He is not asking you to call evil good.
He is calling you to refuse to let evil become your master.
Romans 12:19 says:
"Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord."
Those words do not mean that wrongdoing should go unchallenged or that victims must remain silent.
They mean that ultimate vengeance belongs to God.
We are not qualified to occupy His throne.
And the longer we cling to that throne, the more our hearts can begin to resemble the very darkness we condemn.
There is another detail in Genesis 4 that deserves our attention.
After the account of Lamech's family, Scripture returns to Adam and Eve.
Genesis 4:25 records the birth of Seth, whom Eve acknowledges as another offspring appointed by God after Abel's death.
Then Genesis 4:26 says that in the days of Enos, people began to call upon the name of the LORD.
The chapter that records Cain's violence and Lamech's alarming boast ends with a reference to calling upon God.
We should not flatten this into a claim that everyone in Seth's family was righteous or everyone in Cain's family was beyond grace. Scripture does not teach that.
But the narrative movement is meaningful.
Human violence does not get the final word in the chapter.
The name of the LORD is still being invoked.
Humanity's story has not been abandoned.
And the Bible will continue unfolding God's promise until it reaches Jesus Christ, the promised Savior.
That is the hope running through Scripture.
Not that human beings will eventually become clever enough to cure their own sin.
Not that civilization will advance until evil disappears.
Not that religious activity alone will repair the human heart.
Our hope is that God acts to redeem what sin has ruined.
And He has acted decisively in His Son.
This is why the theme of Gospel Warrior matters so deeply to me.
Not because the scandal never happened.
Not because sin has no consequences.
Not because forgiveness erases every earthly wound or instantly restores broken trust.
But because the grace of Jesus Christ can bring genuine repentance, forgiveness, and transformation into lives that once seemed beyond hope.
The angry can learn gentleness.
The proud can be humbled.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The bitter can begin to heal.
The wounded can find strength to pursue truth without surrendering to hatred.
And the sinner who comes to Christ in repentance and faith can receive a new identity that is not defined by the darkest chapter of their past.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."
That promise is not about pretending the past never existed.
It is about the transforming reality of belonging to Jesus.
And maybe tonight, your most important decision is not to win another argument.
Maybe it is to stop feeding the resentment that has been eating your soul.
Maybe it is to confess the pride you have been calling strength.
Maybe it is to ask forgiveness from someone you wounded.
Maybe it is to tell a trusted pastor, mature believer, or counselor that you are struggling with anger you no longer know how to control.
Maybe it is to establish a necessary boundary without hatred.
Maybe it is to kneel before Jesus and admit that you cannot change your heart by willpower alone.
You need His grace.
You need His truth.
You need the Holy Spirit to produce in you what bitterness never could.
And if you have never truly surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, the invitation is not merely to admire His teachings.
It is to turn from sin and trust in the crucified and risen Savior.
He died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures.
And everyone who turns to Him in genuine faith finds a Savior who is mighty to save.
That is the Gospel.
Not self-improvement dressed in religious language.
Not a motivational message that leaves sin untouched.
Not a promise that every earthly problem will disappear.
But reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ, forgiveness of sins, and the gift of new life.
And I want to ask you something personal.
When you read Lamech's words, did you immediately think of someone else?
Someone arrogant?
Someone cruel?
Someone who wounded you?
I understand why.
But before you close this article, consider one more question.
Is there any part of Lamech's spirit that you have been protecting inside yourself?
That refusal to apologize.
That need to win.
That secret satisfaction when someone who hurt you suffers.
That habit of making your pain the justification for hurting others.
If the Holy Spirit is exposing something, do not run from His conviction.
Bring it to Jesus.
You do not have to publish the details of your struggle for strangers to see. Some wounds require privacy, protection, and trusted support.
Your story may encourage someone who believes change is no longer possible.
Someone reading quietly may need to know they are not the only believer still fighting a battle against resentment.
Someone may need to hear that repentance is not humiliation before a cruel God.
It is returning to the merciful Savior who receives sinners.
And someone may be one honest prayer away from beginning a long-overdue journey toward healing.
Not because every sentence is comfortable.
But because there may come a day when an old wound opens again, and you need to remember that revenge is not the only path available.
A simple share can carry Scripture into the life of a person we may never meet.
Someone who has stopped attending church.
Someone whose marriage is breaking under the weight of bitterness.
Someone who is furious at God.
Someone who has been silently wondering whether Jesus could ever forgive what they have done.
And if you have been strengthened by this ministry, I want to invite you to consider something more personal.
Gospel Warrior is not simply trying to publish another article that people read today and forget tomorrow.
Our desire is to keep placing the Word of God before people who are hungry for truth, struggling with sin, searching for hope, and longing to know Jesus more deeply.
That requires continued writing, research, biblical study, preparation, resource development, and the support of people who believe this mission is worth sustaining.
God's grace cannot be purchased.
And nobody should feel that they must pay a ministry to prove their love for Jesus.
But when believers freely and cheerfully support faithful Gospel work, that generosity can become a meaningful expression of love for God and neighbor.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
"God loveth a cheerful giver."
Not a pressured giver.
Not a frightened giver.
A cheerful giver.
These products are not the reason to follow Christ, and the discount is not the heart of this invitation.
It is simply one practical way we want to thank those who help sustain the ministry.
Explore the resources.
Study the Scriptures.
Share what strengthens your faith.
Encourage someone else to begin reading God's Word.
Every person reached is a person worth loving.
Every soul matters.
Every opportunity to point someone toward Jesus is worth taking seriously.
And before we finish, I want to return to the two women standing at the beginning of this story.
Adah.
Zillah.
We do not know what passed through their minds when Lamech spoke.
The Bible does not tell us whether they were frightened, impressed, troubled, or silent.
We should not invent their emotions.
But we do know what Scripture preserved.
A man's words.
A man's claim of killing.
A man's extraordinary declaration of vengeance.
And generations later, we are still hearing his voice.
That alone should make us consider the legacy of our own words.
What will the people closest to us remember?
Will our children remember the sound of our anger more clearly than the tenderness of our prayers?
Will our spouse remember that we always needed to be right, or that we knew how to repent?
Will our friends remember that we could destroy people with our words, or that we spoke truth with love?
Will those who know us see a person obsessed with personal vindication, or someone learning to reflect the mercy of Christ?
None of us will answer those questions perfectly.
That is precisely why we need Jesus.
We need Him when we have been wounded.
We need Him when we have wounded others.
We need Him when our pride is loud.
We need Him when our conscience is troubled.
We need Him when forgiveness feels impossible.
We need Him when repentance feels costly.
And we need Him when we discover that the person most desperately in need of God's mercy is the one looking back at us in the mirror.
Lamech's words remind us how far the human heart can wander when pride and vengeance take control.
The cross reminds us how far God's love has gone to redeem sinners.
And the empty tomb declares that sin and death do not have the final victory over those who belong to Christ.
So do not leave this story merely shocked by Lamech.
Leave it examining your own heart.
Leave it grateful for the mercy of Jesus.
Leave it willing to repent.
Leave it determined to pursue justice without becoming enslaved to revenge.
And leave it remembering that the greatest answer to humanity's darkness was not another human boast.
It was the crucified and risen Son of God.
Lamech wanted the world to remember how fiercely he could avenge a wound. Jesus wants the wounded world to discover how completely His grace can change a heart.
